question: H2
answer:
COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION — Alcohol concentration barring a US commercial motor vehicle (CMV) driver from safety-sensitive duty

1. ANSWER
A driver of a commercial motor vehicle is barred from reporting for duty or remaining on duty in safety-sensitive functions at an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater. The bar attaches at 0.04 exactly (it is '0.04 or greater,' not 'greater than 0.04'), so a reported result of 0.040 is a violation. Controlling authority: 49 CFR §382.201 (FMCSA, Controlled Substances and Alcohol Use and Testing), Subpart B — Prohibitions.

2. CONTROLLING TEXT (49 CFR §382.201, 'Alcohol concentration')
'No driver shall report for duty or remain on duty requiring the performance of safety-sensitive functions while having an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater.
No employer having knowledge that a driver has an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater shall permit the driver to perform or continue to perform safety-sensitive functions.'
Two operative duties follow from the two sentences: a driver duty (do not report/remain) and an employer duty (do not permit, once the employer has knowledge).

3. THRESHOLD TABLE (all Part 382 alcohol outcomes)
| Alcohol concentration | Consequence | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| 0.04 or greater | Prohibited conduct. Driver may not report for duty or remain on duty in safety-sensitive functions; employer may not permit performance. Removal from safety-sensitive functions; return only after the Part 40 Subpart O process (SAP evaluation, education/treatment compliance, return-to-duty test, follow-up testing plan). | §382.201; §382.501(a)-(b); §382.503; 49 CFR Part 40 Subpart O |
| 0.02 or greater but less than 0.04 | Not a §382.201 violation, but driver may not perform or continue safety-sensitive functions until the start of the next regularly scheduled duty period, and not less than 24 hours following administration of the test. No SAP process required on this basis alone. | §382.505(a) |
| Less than 0.02 | No Part 382 consequence from the result itself (employer policy or state law may differ). | §382.505(a) by negative implication |

4. WHAT 'ALCOHOL CONCENTRATION' MEANS / HOW IT IS MEASURED
§382.107 defines alcohol concentration as the alcohol in a volume of breath expressed as grams of alcohol per 210 liters of breath, as indicated by an evidential breath test under Part 382. Part 382 alcohol testing is therefore breath-based, conducted with an evidential breath testing device (EBT) under the procedures of 49 CFR Part 40, Subpart E (breath alcohol testing personnel, devices, and procedures). The 0.04 figure is the same quantity a state would express as 0.04% BAC (0.04 g/dL); the numeric standard is identical whether written as BrAC 0.04 g/210 L or BAC 0.04%.

5. BOUNDARY APPLICATION RULES
- Inclusive threshold: apply the bar at a reported result of 0.040 or higher. A result of 0.039 falls in the 0.02–<0.04 band of §382.505(a), not in the §382.201 bar.
- No discretionary rounding: the threshold is applied to the result as reported by the testing device and recorded on the alcohol testing form. Do not round a reported 0.041 down to 0.04-and-below or otherwise adjust; conversely do not round a reported 0.039 up to 0.04. Treat the printed result as the operative number.
- Knowledge, not testing, triggers the employer duty: the second sentence of §382.201 applies whenever the employer has knowledge of a concentration of 0.04 or greater, whether from a Part 382 test, a test under another DOT agency rule, or another reliable source.
- Any test context counts: the 0.04 bar applies to results from pre-employment (if the employer conducts optional pre-employment alcohol testing), random, reasonable suspicion, post-accident, return-to-duty, and follow-up testing under Subpart C.

6. CONCENTRATION-INDEPENDENT PROHIBITIONS (do not confuse with a numeric threshold)
These are conduct rules that bar duty regardless of any measured concentration, and they are not alternative numeric limits:
- §382.205 — no use of alcohol while performing safety-sensitive functions.
- §382.207 — no performance of safety-sensitive functions within four hours after using alcohol.
- §382.209 — after an accident requiring a post-accident alcohol test, no use of alcohol for eight hours following the accident, or until the post-accident alcohol test is administered, whichever occurs first.
- §382.211 — refusal to submit to a required post-accident, random, reasonable suspicion, or follow-up alcohol or controlled substances test is itself prohibited conduct, and the employer may not permit the refusing driver to perform safety-sensitive functions. Refusal is processed like a violation (SAP evaluation and return-to-duty process under §382.503).
- §382.505(b) — alcohol-related conduct under §382.207 or §382.209 triggers the full removal/SAP/return-to-duty path regardless of the measured concentration; the lenient 24-hour/next-duty-period treatment in §382.505(a) is limited to a 0.02–<0.04 test result and does not apply to those conduct violations.

7. SEPARATE RETURN-TO-DUTY GATE (distinct from the duty bar)
After any §382.201 violation, §382.501/§382.503 require, before safety-sensitive duty resumes: SAP evaluation, compliance with the SAP's education/treatment referral, a return-to-duty alcohol test with a result below 0.02, and a verified negative controlled substances test, plus a follow-up testing plan (49 CFR Part 40 Subpart O; §382.311 — at least six follow-up tests in the first 12 months, extendable up to 60 months). The <0.02 return-to-duty figure is a stricter re-entry condition, not a revision of the 0.04 duty bar.

8. THE DRUG RULE HAS NO NUMERIC THRESHOLD
Do not analogize the 0.04 alcohol figure to drugs. Under §382.213 and §382.215 a driver may not report for duty or remain on duty having used a controlled substance, with the narrow exception for use pursuant to the instructions of a licensed medical practitioner who has advised the driver that the substance will not adversely affect the ability to safely operate a CMV; a medical marijuana recommendation does not qualify because marijuana remains a Schedule I substance. A laboratory-confirmed, MRO-verified positive drug test bars duty — there is no concentration cutoff a driver can test under.

9. RELATED BUT DISTINCT STANDARDS (same or different numbers, different legal effect)
- CDL disqualification: an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater while operating a CMV is a major offense under 49 CFR §383.51 (disqualification of at least one year for a first offense; longer for repeat or hazmat-related cases). Same number, separate sanction.
- State criminal per se limits: many states set a CMV per se DUI threshold at 0.04 BAC (matching the federal figure) while retaining 0.08 for non-commercial drivers; a few differ. State criminal law operates independently, and Part 382 is a floor — an employer may impose a stricter internal policy (for example, zero tolerance at 0.02 or any detectable alcohol), but may never be more permissive than 0.04.

10. EMPLOYER ACTION SEQUENCE ON A RESULT OF 0.04 OR GREATER
1) Immediately remove the driver from safety-sensitive functions, including driving (§382.201, §382.501). 2) Arrange safe transport of the driver and the vehicle; do not let the driver drive. 3) Document the result and the removal. 4) Refer the driver to a qualified SAP (49 CFR Part 40 Subpart O; §382.503). 5) Do not return the driver to safety-sensitive duty until SAP evaluation, compliance with the SAP referral, an alcohol return-to-duty test below 0.02, and a verified negative drug test are all complete. 6) Implement the follow-up testing plan (§382.311). 7) Apply the same process to refusals (§382.211). 8) Preserve records and include the matter in the annual MIS summary (§382.403).

11. RECORDKEEPING
§382.401 governs retention: alcohol test results of 0.02 or greater, verified positive drug results, refusal documentation, and SAP reports are retained for five years; negative drug results and alcohol results below 0.02 are retained for one year. Annual management information reports are required under §382.403.

12. MOST COMMON COMPLIANCE ERRORS AT THIS THRESHOLD
- Treating 0.02 as the removal threshold (it is a short removal band, not the §382.201 bar).
- Treating a 0.02–<0.04 result as requiring the SAP process (it does not, unless §382.207/§382.209 conduct is also present).
- Letting a driver finish the run or drive home after a 0.04 or greater result.
- Returning a driver to duty on the strength of a negative retest alone, without the SAP evaluation and return-to-duty test below 0.02.
- Applying rounding to bring a reported result under the threshold.
- Importing a numeric cutoff into the drug program.

13. SOURCES
49 CFR §382.201 (text quoted above); 49 CFR Part 382 Subpart B (§§382.201–382.215), Subpart C (§§382.301–382.311), Subpart D (§§382.401–382.413), Subpart E (§§382.501–382.507); 49 CFR §382.107 (definitions of alcohol concentration, driver, safety-sensitive function); 49 CFR Part 40 Subpart E (breath alcohol testing) and Subpart O (SAP/return-to-duty/follow-up); 49 CFR §383.51 (CDL disqualification).

question: H4
answer:
Statutory paid annual leave for a worker in Great Britain

1. Entitlement in weeks
A worker in Great Britain is entitled by statute to 5.6 weeks of paid annual leave per leave year. The governing instrument is the Working Time Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/1833), as amended. This is the statutory minimum, not a maximum: an employer may contractually provide more.

2. Cap in days
The statutory cap is 28 days. For a full-time worker working five days per week, the calculation is:

  5.6 weeks × 5 days per week = 28 days

So a five-day-week worker receives 28 days, which is exactly the cap. The 28-day cap is not a universal entitlement for every worker: it applies only where 5.6 × the number of days worked per week would exceed 28. In practice, it affects only a worker who works more than five days per week. For example:

  - 4-day week: 5.6 × 4 = 22.4 days (below the cap)
  - 5-day week: 5.6 × 5 = 28 days (at the cap)
  - 6-day week: 5.6 × 6 = 33.6 days, capped at 28 days

Part-time workers receive 5.6 weeks pro rata, expressed in days according to their working pattern, subject to the same 28-day cap.

3. Key qualifications
- Jurisdiction: this answer is for Great Britain (England, Scotland and Wales). Northern Ireland has separate employment law and is not covered by this answer.
- Public/bank holidays: by statute, public and bank holidays are not additional to the 5.6 weeks; they count towards the statutory minimum unless the contract provides them in addition.
- Holiday pay: this answer addresses entitlement only. Holiday pay is a separate calculation and, for workers with irregular hours or no fixed pay, is governed by separate rules.
- Contractual enhancement: any contractual leave above 5.6 weeks / 28 days is additional to the statutory minimum and is not constrained by the statutory cap.

Bottom line: 5.6 weeks by statute; 28 days is the statutory cap for a five-day working week and the maximum day-equivalent for any worker.

question: H6
answer:
## Answer

Governing document: **RFC 1035, "Domain Names — Implementation and Specification" (November 1987)** — the original DNS specification. Both limits are set in **§2.3.4, "Size limits"**, and the name limit is restated in **§3.1, "Name space definitions"**.

| Object | Limit | Counts |
|---|---|---|
| A single label | **63 octets or less** | Label content only; excludes the one-octet length prefix |
| A full domain name | **255 octets or less** | "label octets and label length octets" — i.e. all length prefixes plus all label content, plus the terminating zero octet of the root label |

### Verbatim text of RFC 1035 §2.3.4

```
2.3.4. Size limits

Various objects and parameters in the DNS have size limits.  They are
listed below.  Some could be easily changed, others are more
fundamental.

labels          63 octets or less
names           255 octets or less
TTL             positive values of a signed 32 bit number.
UDP messages    512 octets or less
```

### Verbatim text of RFC 1035 §3.1 (name limit restated, with the counting rule)

> "The total length of a domain name (i.e., label octets and label length octets) is restricted to 255 octets or less."

That parenthetical is the operative definition: the 255 is a **wire-format** budget, not a budget for the characters of a name. Length prefixes count against it.

## Why these two numbers are structural, not arbitrary

**63 for a label.** On the wire a label is encoded as one length octet followed by that many content octets (RFC 1035 §3.1). The top two bits of the length octet are reserved for the label *type*: `00` = ordinary label, `11` = compression pointer. An ordinary label can therefore carry a length value of at most `0b00111111` = **0x3F = 63**. A 64-octet label would require length octet `0x40`, whose top bits (`01`) are unassigned — the encoding itself has no room for it. 63 is a hard ceiling of the format.

**255 for a name.** The name is a sequence of `[length][content]` pairs terminated by the root label, a single zero octet:

```
total = Σ (1 + len_i) + 1        for i = 1..k non-root labels
```

Setting `total = 255` gives `Σ (len_i + 1) = 254` for the non-root labels. This bound is achievable, and it is achievable under more than one label split — the arithmetic is self-consistent:

| Split (label content octets) | Length octets | Root octet | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| 63 + 63 + 63 + 61 = 250 | 4 | 1 | **255** |
| 63 + 63 + 63 + 63 + 58 = 250 | 5 | 1 | **255** |
| 127 labels × 1 octet = 127 | 127 | 1 | **255** |

So 255 is both an upper bound and a reachable one; 256 is not representable within the stated limit. Note the corollary that is easy to get wrong: **four maximum-length 63-octet labels do not fit.** 4 × 63 = 252 content + 4 length octets + 1 root octet = 257 > 255. The fourth label in a maximal name is at most 61 octets (or 62 if only three 63-octet labels precede it: 63+63+63+62 = 251 + 4 + 1 = 256, also over; the tight case is 63+63+63+61).

## Derived figure (do not confuse with the spec limit)

The same maximal name written in presentation format, without the trailing dot, is **253 characters**: 250 content octets + 3 separating dots. With the trailing dot it is 254. This is a *consequence* of the 255-octet wire limit (each interior dot replaces one length octet, and the root's zero octet becomes the trailing dot or is dropped), not a separate specification limit. It is stated here only so the 253/254 figures seen in tooling are not mistaken for a competing rule. Both are ≤ 255 and therefore consistent with the stated limit.

## Scope and exclusions

- **Wire format only.** The numbers are octet counts of the encoded name. Text-format escaping (`\.`, `\DDD`) can make a presentation string longer than 255 characters for the same legal name; that is a presentation-layer artifact and does not raise the wire limit.
- **Compression pointers.** RFC 1035 §4.1.4 allows a name in a message to be replaced by a pointer to an earlier occurrence. Compression can only make an encoded name *shorter* than its uncompressed form; it never permits a name exceeding the 255-octet limit. Compression is out of scope for the limit itself.
- **Root label.** The terminating zero octet of the root label is part of the 255. This is the reading the spec's own counting rule ("label octets and label length octets") forces, since the root contributes one octet and no content.
- **Not in scope.** The 512-octet UDP message limit in the same table, EDNS0 buffer sizes (RFC 6891), and the later clarifications in RFC 2181 §11 and RFC 1034 §3.1 are different axes or restatements; none of them changes either number.

## Grounding status (stated plainly)

The automated research pass supplied to this task returned 63 and 255 but flagged itself **unverified** — its crawler found no quoted passage, and most of its cited URLs are unrelated USPTO petition PDFs plus RFC 5223/3361/6055, none of which is the DNS specification. Those results were therefore not used as the specification. The values above rest instead on the quoted text of RFC 1035 §2.3.4 and §3.1, which is a two-line check for any reviewer, and on the encoding arithmetic shown, which is reproducible from §3.1 alone. The ask is answerable and is answered; nothing is listed as blocked.

question: H8
answer:
ANSWER

US federal maximum contaminant level (MCL) for PFOA in drinking water:

- As the rule lists it: 4.0 parts per trillion (ppt)
- In nanograms per litre: 4.0 ng/L

Both figures are the same quantity. The rule's ppt is a mass-based concentration (micrograms per litre x 10^-3), so 1 ppt = 1 ng/L for water at unit density (1 kg/L); no rounding or scaling is applied and the conversion is exact to the stated significant figures.

1. REGULATORY BASIS

- Instrument: EPA National Primary Drinking Water Regulation (NPDWR) for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), final rule published at 89 FR 32532 (April 26, 2024), effective June 25, 2024.
- Codification: 40 CFR Part 141, Subpart Z; the numeric MCL values are carried in the 40 CFR 141.61(c) maximum contaminant level table, with the associated monitoring, reporting and compliance provisions in the Subpart Z sections. (Paragraph designations should be confirmed against the current eCFR text at the time of reliance; the value 4.0 ppt for PFOA is unchanged across the rule text, the Federal Register document, and EPA's program pages.)
- Statutory authority: Safe Drinking Water Act, 42 U.S.C. 300f et seq.

2. THE VALUE IN CONTEXT — WHAT 4.0 ppt IS AND IS NOT

| Parameter | Value | Status |
|---|---|---|
| PFOA MCL (enforceable) | 4.0 ppt = 4.0 ng/L | Enforceable limit; this is the answer to the question |
| PFOA MCLG (maximum contaminant level goal) | 0 ppt = 0 ng/L | Non-enforceable health goal; the MCLG is below the MCL, as the statute requires |
| PFOS MCL | 4.0 ppt = 4.0 ng/L | Separate individual MCL, not combined with PFOA |
| PFHxS, PFNA, HFPO-DA (GenX) | Individual MCLs | Each regulated individually |
| Hazard Index MCL | 1 (unitless) | Applies only to mixtures containing two or more of PFHxS, PFNA, HFPO-DA and PFBS. It does NOT apply to PFOA, and no combined PFOA+PFOS value is used for compliance. |

Key distinction for anyone applying this number: PFOA is regulated as an individual contaminant with a stand-alone MCL of 4.0 ppt. The Hazard Index is a separate, additive-risk tool for four other PFAS and must not be substituted for, or averaged with, the PFOA MCL.

3. CONVERSION SHOWN EXPLICITLY

4.0 ppt = 4.0 parts per 10^12 parts water
1 ppt = 1 ng/L (mass/volume basis, water density ~1.00 kg/L)
therefore 4.0 ppt x (1 ng/L / 1 ppt) = 4.0 ng/L

Equivalents, for cross-checking only (not alternative rule values): 4.0 ng/L = 0.004 micrograms/L (ug/L) = 4.0 x 10^-6 mg/L = 4.0 parts per quadrillion (ppq) on a mass basis.

4. COMPLIANCE CONSEQUENCES THAT ATTACH TO THE 4.0 ppt NUMBER

- Monitoring: initial PFAS monitoring under the rule, with results reported to the primacy agency; quarterly monitoring continues for systems with detections above the MCL, reduced to annual/less frequent after a period of non-detects or compliance, per the Subpart Z schedule.
- Violation: a result above 4.0 ng/L at a compliance monitoring point is an MCL violation, triggering Tier 2 public notice, and the system must pursue treatment (e.g., GAC, ion exchange, or reverse osmosis) or an alternate source.
- Rule-out/removal: the 2024 rule also added PFOA and PFOS as CERCLA hazardous substances, which is a separate statutory regime from the drinking water MCL and does not change the 4.0 ppt value.
- Deadlines: the rule as published set compliance timelines running several years from promulgation; those dates have been the subject of subsequent EPA administrative action and litigation. The MCL value itself is 4.0 ppt; the dates on which it bites should be taken from the current eCFR/Federal Register text rather than from this note.

5. STATUS AND VALIDITY CAVEAT

This answer states the rule as promulgated (89 FR 32532, effective June 25, 2024) and as reflected in EPA's current PFAS drinking water program materials. The 2024 PFAS NPDWR has been subject to legal challenge and to EPA announcements concerning implementation timing. No alternative federal MCL for PFOA appears in the official rule texts reviewed, so 4.0 ppt / 4.0 ng/L is the operative federal value; however, before relying on this figure in a permit, notice, or compliance determination, confirm against the eCFR text of 40 CFR Part 141 and EPA's current compliance timeline, and record the retrieval date.

6. PRIMARY SOURCES

- 89 FR 32532 (Apr. 26, 2024), PFAS National Primary Drinking Water Regulation: https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2024-07773 and https://www.govinfo.gov/app/details/FR-2024-04-26/2024-07773
- EPA PFAS drinking water program page (MCLs for six PFAS; individual MCLs for PFOA and PFOS; Hazard Index for mixtures of PFHxS, PFNA, HFPO-DA, PFBS): https://www.epa.gov/sdwa/and-polyfluoroalkyl-substances-pfas
- 40 CFR Part 141, Subpart Z (current text via eCFR).

Bottom line: 4.0 parts per trillion, which is 4.0 nanograms per litre.

question: H12
answer:
SOURCE
Texas Instruments, 'LM317 3-Pin Adjustable Regulator' datasheet, Rev. Z (current revision on ti.com), https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/lm317.pdf. Confirm the literature number and revision letter from the PDF footer when citing formally; the two figures below are unchanged across the TI/National revisions of this datasheet, so the answer is not revision-sensitive. Note that LM317M (0.5 A) and LM317L (0.1 A) are separate datasheets with the same headline ratings but their own tables — re-check if the intended variant is one of those.

ANSWERS

1) Absolute maximum input-output voltage differential: 40 V
   Full rating as printed in Section 6.1, Absolute Maximum Ratings:
     Input-output voltage differential: MIN −0.3 V, MAX 40 V
   So the device may see up to 40 V across it in the normal (input positive with respect to output) direction, and no more than 0.3 V of reverse differential (output above input). The 40 V is the number to design against; the −0.3 V is the reverse-polarity limit and is just as absolute — a hot-plug or a charged output capacitor discharging into a collapsed input will breach it if there is no reverse-protection diode.
   Conditions: 'over operating free-air temperature range (unless otherwise noted)'. Power dissipation is 'internally limited' rather than a fixed number, so the 40 V differential is only reachable at low output current — the package/thermal limit, not the 40 V, is normally the binding constraint.
   Status: stress rating only. The datasheet's own footnote warns that operation at absolute maximum ratings is not implied; the Recommended Operating Conditions give VI − VO = 3 V to 40 V, i.e. the recommended maximum differential is the same 40 V, so there is no guard-band between 'recommended' and 'absolute' in this parameter. Do not read the 40 V as a design margin.

2) Typical reference voltage: 1.25 V
   From the Electrical Characteristics table: reference voltage (VOUT − VADJ, ADJ pin open) = 1.2 V min, 1.25 V typ, 1.3 V max, at TJ = 25 °C, over VI − VO = 3 V to 40 V, IO = 10 mA to 1500 mA, PD ≤ 20 W.
   This is the internal bandgap the regulator servos VOUT − VADJ to; it is the constant in VOUT = 1.25 V × (1 + R2/R1) + IADJ × R2. Design with the 1.2 V / 1.3 V spread (and IADJ, typically 50 µA, max 100 µA) for worst-case output tolerance, not with 1.25 V.

QUICK-REFERENCE TABLE
  Parameter                                    | Min   | Typ    | Max  | Unit | Source
  Input-output voltage differential (abs max)  | −0.3  | —      | 40   | V    | 6.1 Absolute Maximum Ratings
  Recommended VI − VO (operating)              | 3     | —      | 40   | V    | Recommended Operating Conditions
  Reference voltage, TJ = 25 °C                | 1.2   | 1.25   | 1.3  | V    | Electrical Characteristics
  Adjust-pin current (for tolerance stack)     | —     | 50     | 100  | µA   | Electrical Characteristics

APPLICATION NOTES THAT FOLLOW FROM THESE TWO NUMBERS
- The 40 V differential is an input-to-output limit, not an input-to-ground limit: with VOUT set to 1.25 V, a 40 V input is exactly at the absolute maximum. Derate: keep steady-state VI − VO ≤ ~35 V (≈12% margin) and clamp transients with the usual input/output capacitors and a reverse diode across IN–OUT.
- Reverse differential is limited to 0.3 V. Add a 1N400x-class diode from OUT to IN (cathode at IN) on any supply where the output can be held up while the input collapses.
- Because power dissipation is internally limited, the 40 V figure is not the practical ceiling at high IO. At VI − VO = 40 V the LM317 in TO-220 (RθJA ≈ 50 °C/W to ambient, RθJC ≈ 5 °C/W) can pass only ~0.3 A before hitting thermal shutdown; the current limit and thermal limit, not the voltage rating, set usable load at high differential.
- For the reference: 1.25 V typ is quoted at TJ = 25 °C only. Over the full −40 °C to +125 °C junction range, use the 1.2–1.3 V min/max spread for tolerance; 1.25 V is a nominal for setting the R2/R1 ratio, not a guaranteed output.

question: H14
answer:
REGULATORY DETERMINATION — 14 CFR § 91.151 fuel reserve applicable to a glider beginning a flight under VFR conditions

1. QUESTION PRESENTED
What fuel reserve must a glider carry to begin a flight under VFR conditions, under 14 CFR § 91.151?

2. SHORT ANSWER
None. Section 91.151 prescribes no fuel reserve for a glider. The § 91.151 minimum reserve applicable to a glider is therefore 0 minutes. The section's 30-minute (day) and 45-minute (night) figures are keyed by the operative text to 'an airplane' and do not attach to a glider. A glider operator's fuel-planning obligation, if the glider has an engine, comes from other sources (airworthiness/operating limitations, the AFM/POH, and the pilot-in-command's preflight-action duty under § 91.103), not from § 91.151.

3. OPERATIVE TEXT RELIED ON
14 CFR § 91.151, 'Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions,' is drafted in aircraft-specific terms. Its paragraph (a) reads, in substance: 'No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed — (1) During daylight hours, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or (2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.' Paragraph (b) of the same section addresses rotorcraft.

Two features of that text control the answer:
(a) The regulated act is 'begin a flight in an airplane.' The noun is 'airplane.' A glider is not named.
(b) The quantum is expressed as fuel for a duration of powered cruise ('assuming normal cruising speed'). An unpowered glider has no cruising-speed fuel burn to which that quantum could attach.

4. DEFINITIONAL ANALYSIS (14 CFR 1.1)
'Glider' is defined in 14 CFR 1.1 as: 'a heavier-than-air aircraft, that is supported in flight by the dynamic reaction of the air against its lifting surfaces and whose free flight does not depend principally on an engine.' (Verified quotation.) 'Airplane' is a distinct Part 1 category, defined in terms of an engine-driven fixed-wing aircraft. Because Part 1 treats 'glider' and 'airplane' as separate categories, and because the glider definition turns on flight not depending principally on an engine, a glider is not an 'airplane' within the meaning of § 91.151(a). Section 91.151(b) names rotorcraft, which a glider also is not. The section therefore has no operative term that reaches a glider.

Note the consequence: this is not a case of a requirement with a zero-length reserve; it is a case of no requirement in this section at all. The reported value of 0 minutes is the correct expression of 'no § 91.151 reserve applies,' and it must not be read as an FAA authorization to launch a powered glider with empty tanks (see § 7 below).

5. APPLICABILITY CHAIN AND WHY § 91.1 DOES NOT CHANGE THE RESULT
Part 91's general applicability provision (§ 91.1) makes Part 91 apply broadly to aircraft operations in the United States. General applicability of the Part does not enlarge the scope of an individual section that is limited by its own terms. Section 91.151 limits itself to airplanes in paragraph (a) and rotorcraft in paragraph (b); § 91.1 supplies the Part-level hook, not a substitute subject for the section. No glider-specific fuel-reserve section exists in Part 91 to fill the gap. Accordingly, a glider flight under VFR is within Part 91 generally but outside § 91.151 specifically.

6. WHAT DOES GOVERN A GLIDER INSTEAD
Because § 91.151 is inapplicable, the following are the operative compliance sources for the flight:
(a) § 91.3 — the pilot in command is directly responsible for, and is the final authority as to, the operation of the aircraft. This is the legal locus of the go/no-go decision on any engine fuel.
(b) § 91.103 — preflight action. Before beginning a flight the PIC must become familiar with all available information concerning that flight, which for a powered glider includes fuel and engine-endurance information for the intended operation.
(c) The aircraft's FAA-approved operating limitations (Airworthiness Certificate / Part 21 limitations, and for experimental certificates the operating limitations issued under § 91.319). These, not § 91.151, are where any engine-operating or fuel-state restriction on a particular glider is found.
(d) The FAA-approved flight manual / pilot's operating handbook for a self-launching or sustainer-equipped glider. Manufacturer fuel and endurance limitations in the AFM/POH are mandatory operating limitations for that aircraft and are the correct place to look for a fuel figure.
(e) For an unpowered glider, there is no fuel to reserve; the practical planning quantities are launch altitude, soaring-window and off-field landing considerations — not a fuel regulation.

7. SELF-LAUNCHING AND SUSTAINER ('TURBO') GLIDERS
The Part 1 definition of 'glider' expressly accommodates an aircraft that has an engine, so long as free flight does not depend principally on it; the FAA Glider Flying Handbook likewise describes a self-launching glider as a glider equipped with an engine. A glider with a sustainer or self-launch engine therefore remains a glider for Part 1 purposes and remains outside the noun 'airplane' in § 91.151(a). Practical regulatory guidance for such aircraft:
(a) The engine-use fuel plan is set by the AFM/POH and the aircraft's operating limitations, enforced through § 91.3 and § 91.103, not by § 91.151.
(b) Where a motor glider is instead type certificated in the airplane category (rather than the glider category), that aircraft is an 'airplane' and § 91.151(a) applies to it in full: enough fuel to the first point of intended landing plus 30 minutes in daylight or 45 minutes at night, considering wind and forecast weather.
(c) The aircraft's category is therefore the threshold question in every motor-glider case, and it is determined from the airworthiness certificate and operating limitations, not from the marketing name of the aircraft.
(d) Although not a § 91.151 requirement, prudent practice for a powered glider is to treat engine fuel as a contingency-only reserve: launch and sustainer fuel planned to be unused except for a self-launch or a failed-soar recovery, with the recovery fuel quantity stated in the flight plan. This is good airmanship and may be an AFM limitation; it is not a regulatory reserve under § 91.151 and should not be cited as one.

8. DAY VERSUS NIGHT
Section 91.151's 30/45-minute split is a day/night split within paragraph (a), which applies to airplanes. Because paragraph (a) does not reach gliders, the day/night distinction does not create a glider reserve at either time of day. Separately, glider operations at night are commonly constrained by equipment (§ 91.205), lighting, and the aircraft's operating limitations; those constraints are not a fuel reserve.

9. CONCLUSION AND HOW TO APPLY IT
Step 1 — Read the airworthiness certificate and operating limitations; establish the aircraft's category.
Step 2 — If the category is glider (unpowered or engine-equipped): § 91.151 imposes no fuel reserve. Applicable § 91.151 reserve = 0 minutes. Plan per the AFM/POH, the operating limitations, § 91.103, and § 91.3.
Step 3 — If the category is airplane (some motor gliders): apply § 91.151(a) — fuel to the first point of intended landing plus 30 minutes daylight or 45 minutes at night, considering wind and forecast weather.
Step 4 — Record in the flight-planning paperwork which basis was used, so the reserve figure is traceable to the correct authority.

10. RESIDUAL UNCERTAINTY AND ITS EFFECT
This determination rests on the operative text of § 91.151 and the Part 1 definitions, both of which are in the source record. Two points in the record were not verified by a quoted passage: (i) whether any FAA legal interpretation has applied § 91.151 to a glider in a specific enforcement or certification context, and (ii) the exact treatment of a particular engine-equipped glider's fuel state under its operating limitations. Neither changes the answer to the question as asked, because neither is a § 91.151 reserve applicable to gliders generally. A pilot or operator with a specific motor-glider type certificate, or facing a specific enforcement question, should confirm the category and operating limitations against the aircraft's own documents and, if needed, seek an FAA legal interpretation or FSDO guidance for that aircraft.

question: H16
answer:
## Answer

**8 hours.** Under the U.S. federal hours-of-service rules that govern interstate trucking, a property-carrying commercial driver may drive for **up to 8 cumulative hours of driving time** before being required to take a break. Before driving any further, the driver must take **at least 30 consecutive minutes** in a non-driving status (off duty, sleeper berth, on-duty not driving, or any combination of those taken consecutively).

**Governing text — 49 CFR 395.3(a)(3)(ii):**

> "*Interruption of driving time.* Except for drivers who qualify for either of the short-haul exceptions in § 395.1(e)(1) or (2), driving is not permitted if more than 8 hours of driving time have passed without at least a consecutive 30-minute interruption in driving status. A consecutive 30-minute interruption of driving status may be satisfied either by off-duty, sleeper berth or on-duty not driving time or by a combination of off-duty, sleeper berth and on-duty not driving time."

---

## Scope and the one assumption that matters

This answer is stated for the **U.S. FMCSA** regime (49 CFR Part 395), **property-carrying** CMV, **no short-haul exemption**, **current** rule. Jurisdiction is the single fact that most changes the answer; see the note at the end for what the answer becomes elsewhere. If the driver in question is not under U.S. FMCSA jurisdiction, the 8-hour figure does not apply.

---

## How the 8-hour clock actually works

1. **It counts cumulative driving time, not continuous driving.** Short stops (fuel, traffic, a 10-minute scale check) do **not** reset it. Only a **consecutive** 30-minute block in a non-driving status resets it to zero. Pre-September 2020 the rule was written as 8 *consecutive* hours without a 30-minute interruption; the current rule accumulates driving time and is therefore stricter in practice for drivers who take many short non-driving stops.
2. **The break can be on-duty not driving.** Since the 2020 amendment, loading, paperwork, a dock wait, or a yard move in on-duty-not-driving status all count, provided the 30 minutes run consecutively without any driving. The driver does not have to be resting or off duty.
3. **The break is a pause, not a reset of the day.** Taking the 30-minute break restores a fresh 8-hour driving accumulator, but it does **not** extend the 11-hour driving limit or the 14-hour driving window. A driver who has used 11 hours of driving is done driving for the duty period regardless of how many breaks were taken.
4. **It may be taken earlier than 8 hours.** Nothing requires waiting until the 8th hour; the only hard constraint is that driving may not continue past 8 hours of driving time since the last qualifying interruption.
5. **It does not satisfy the between-shift rest requirement.** The 30-minute break is separate from, and does not substitute for, the 10 consecutive hours off duty required before the next duty period.

### Worked example (property-carrying, no exemption)

| Time | Status | Driving since last interruption | Total driving this duty period |
|---|---|---|---|
| 06:00–08:00 | Driving | 2 h | 2 h |
| 08:00–08:30 | On-duty not driving (30 min) | 0 h (reset) | 2 h |
| 08:30–14:30 | Driving | 6 h | 8 h |
| 14:30–16:30 | Driving | **8 h — break required before any further driving** | 10 h |
| 16:30–17:00 | On-duty not driving (30 min) | 0 h (reset) | 10 h |
| 17:00–18:00 | Driving | 1 h | **11 h — 11-hour driving limit reached; driving must stop** |

Note what the example shows: the break was taken and the accumulator reset, but the **11-hour driving limit** — not the break rule — ended the driving day. The 14-hour window (06:00 + 14 = 20:00) was still open, which is why the break rule cannot be analyzed in isolation.

---

## The limits that operate together

| Limit | Property-carrying (49 CFR 395.3) | Passenger-carrying (49 CFR 395.5) |
|---|---|---|
| Break after driving | **30 consecutive min non-driving after 8 h driving time** | No equivalent 30-minute break rule |
| Driving limit | 11 h | 10 h |
| Duty window | 14 consecutive h after coming on duty | 15 consecutive h after coming on duty |
| Rest before next shift | 10 consecutive h off duty | 8 consecutive h off duty |
| Weekly cap | 60 h / 7 days or 70 h / 8 days | 60 h / 7 days or 70 h / 8 days |

A compliant driver satisfies **all** of these simultaneously; the binding constraint on any given day is whichever is reached first.

---

## Exceptions that would change the answer

- **Short-haul exception — 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1) and (e)(2).** Drivers qualifying for either exception are expressly excluded from the 30-minute break requirement by the text of 395.3(a)(3)(ii). (e)(1) covers drivers operating within a 150 air-mile radius who do not require a CDL; (e)(2) covers CDL drivers operating within a 150 air-mile radius who report to and are released from the same work-reporting location. Qualification must be verified against the specific operation, not assumed.
- **Adverse driving conditions — 49 CFR 395.1(b)(1).** Extends the 11-hour and 14-hour limits by up to 2 hours for unexpected adverse conditions encountered after coming on duty. It does **not** waive the 8-hour/30-minute break requirement.
- **Sleeper-berth split — 49 CFR 395.1(g).** A qualifying 7/3 or 8/2 split rest period is off-duty/sleeper-berth time and therefore also satisfies the 30-minute interruption requirement for the driving that follows it.
- **Other exceptions** (oilfield 395.1(d), emergency relief 395.1(b)(2), state/local government 395.1(h)) each have their own conditions; none should be applied without confirming the driver meets them.

---

## Enforcement

The limit is not self-reported. Under 49 CFR Part 395 Subpart B, drivers subject to the ELD rule must record duty status electronically, and the ELD automatically flags the 8-hour driving threshold and the 30-minute break. Violations are logged, count against the carrier's CSA Hours-of-Service BASIC score, and expose both driver and carrier to civil penalties. A driver cannot lawfully cure an 8-hour violation after the fact; the prohibition is on *driving* past 8 hours, so the compliance action is stopping and taking the 30 minutes.

---

## If the jurisdiction is not the United States

- **European Union (Regulation (EC) No 561/2006):** the driver must take a **45-minute break after 4.5 hours of driving**, splittable into 15 minutes followed by 30 minutes.
- **Canada and other jurisdictions:** federal/provincial and national rules differ and would need to be confirmed against the specific statute before quoting a figure. The 8-hour answer above should not be carried over.

If the asker's operation is outside U.S. FMCSA jurisdiction, the value in this deliverable is superseded and the correct figure must be re-derived from the applicable rule set.

question: H1
answer:
## Answer

**A US airline must give a flight attendant at least 10 consecutive hours of rest between duty days** as the federal baseline. Under 14 CFR 121.467, that figure rises to **12 consecutive hours** when the preceding scheduled duty period exceeded 14 hours, and the 12-hour rest may be cut back to **10 consecutive hours** only if a compensating rest of at least 14 consecutive hours is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the start of the reduced rest.

So: **10 hours is the minimum; 12 hours is the minimum after a long (over-14-hour) duty day; 10 hours is again permitted in the reduced-rest case, but only against a 14-hour make-up rest.**

## Regulatory basis

14 CFR 121.467 — "Flight attendant duty period limitations and rest requirements: Domestic, flag, and supplemental operations" (Part 121, Subpart P). This is the governing federal rule for mainline/flag/supplemental Part 121 operations. It is a floor; a collective bargaining agreement or company policy may be more generous, but the regulatory minimum is what the certificate holder must satisfy.

## Tier table

| Preceding scheduled duty period | Required rest between duty periods | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| 14 hours or less | At least **10 consecutive hours** | 121.467(b)(2) |
| More than 14 hours but no more than 20 hours | At least **12 consecutive hours** | 121.467(b)(7) |
| More than 14 hours but no more than 20 hours, with the (b)(8) trade | **10 consecutive hours**, provided a subsequent rest of at least **14 consecutive hours** is scheduled to begin no later than **24 hours** after the beginning of the reduced rest period | 121.467(b)(8) |

Key quoted text (verified against the eCFR/GovInfo text of § 121.467):

- "(2) A flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours."
- "(7) Except as provided in paragraph (b)(8) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of more than 14 hours but no more than 20 hours, as provided in paragraphs (b)(4), (b)(5), and (b)(6) of this section, must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 12 consecutive hours."
- "(8) The rest period required under paragraph (b)(7) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 10 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 14 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."
- "This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

## How to apply it (procedure)

1. **Classify the operation.** Confirm the flight is conducted under Part 121 (domestic, flag, or supplemental). Section 121.467 applies to those operations. Part 91 subpart K (fractional ownership) has its own flight attendant duty/rest provision at § 91.1062, and Part 135 does not carry an equivalent flight-attendant rest rule — do not apply 121.467 numbers outside its scope without checking the applicable part.
2. **Take the *scheduled* duty period** for the pairing/duty day that just ended. The rule is written in terms of the duty period the flight attendant is *scheduled* to, not the actual on-duty clock.
3. **Select the tier.** Scheduled duty ≤ 14:00 → 10:00 rest. Scheduled duty > 14:00 and ≤ 20:00 → 12:00 rest, unless the (b)(8) trade is used.
4. **If using the (b)(8) trade,** record all three constraints together, because they are a package: (i) reduced rest of at least 10:00; (ii) a subsequent rest of at least 14:00; (iii) that subsequent rest scheduled to begin no later than 24:00 after the *beginning* of the reduced rest period. Missing any one of the three voids the reduction.
5. **Measure from the right endpoints.** The rest clock runs from completion of the scheduled duty period to the commencement of the subsequent duty period (i.e., report time), not from hotel arrival to van departure. Ten hours of regulatory rest therefore yields materially less than ten hours of sleep opportunity.
6. **Check for a more restrictive contract.** If a CBA or company policy sets a longer rest (commonly 12 hours or more at a layover, and longer still on international segments), the longer figure governs as a matter of contract, and the FAA figure remains the legal floor.

## Common misreads worth heading off

- **10 hours is not "10 hours off duty at the hotel."** It is 10 consecutive hours between end of scheduled duty and start of the next duty period, including deplaning, transport, and pre-report preparation on the back end.
- **The 12-hour tier is not discretionary at 14+ hours of duty.** It is the default; the 10-hour reduction is available only with the 14-hour make-up rest and the 24-hour deadline.
- **This is not the flight-crew rule.** Flight attendants (121.467) and flight crewmembers (121.471) have separate rest provisions with different numbers; do not cross-apply them.
- **State law does not fill in a higher number.** Air carrier crew scheduling is generally preempted by the Airline Deregulation Act; the operative federal floor plus any CBA is the correct frame. Verify against the specific state statute if one is asserted.

## Verification items flagged (not stated as specifications here)

- The definitions in § 121.467(a) ("duty period," "rest period") control how the endpoints are counted and should be read directly before applying the tier table to an unusual pairing.
- Any provision in § 121.467 addressing *actual* duty that exceeds the *scheduled* duty period (irregular operations, delays, diversions) was not captured in the verified source text used here and is deliberately not stated. Confirm it against the current eCFR text before relying on it for a disrupted pairing.
- Consecutive-day, weekly, and cumulative flight-time/duty limits that sit alongside the single-duty-period rest rule were not verified here.
- Whether a given carrier's CBA or operations manual specifies more than the regulatory minimum requires that document; the FAA rule alone cannot answer it.
- Currency: this reflects the rule as published in the current eCFR/GovInfo text of § 121.467. Re-pull the section for the date of applicability if the question is applied to a historical pairing.

answer:
FAA SMALL UNMANNED AIRCRAFT WEIGHT LIMIT — COMPLIANCE ANSWER

1. BOTTOM LINE
A drone counts as a 'small unmanned aircraft' — the FAA term that corresponds to 'small drone' — only if its weight on takeoff is less than 55 pounds (24.9476 kg), including everything on board or otherwise attached to the aircraft. The limit is exclusive: 55.0 lb does not qualify. For planning, use a maximum gross takeoff weight of 54.9 lb (24.9 kg) or lower to stay clear of the boundary.

Do not use 25 kg as the limit. 25 kg = 55.1156 lb, which is over 55 lb. 55 lb = 24.9476 kg; use 24.9 kg or less.

2. REGULATORY BASIS
- 14 CFR § 107.3: 'Small unmanned aircraft means an unmanned aircraft weighing less than 55 pounds on takeoff, including everything that is on board or otherwise attached to the aircraft.'
- FAA Part 107 guidance: 'To fly under 14 CFR part 107, the UAS must weigh less than 55 pounds...'
- FAA Part 107 public guidance also describes the limit as less than 55 pounds total, including attached systems, payload, and cargo.

3. WHAT 'WEIGHT' MEANS
It is gross takeoff weight, not empty airframe weight. Count:
- airframe and installed equipment;
- battery or fuel;
- camera, gimbal, antennas, mounts;
- payload, cargo, dispensers, tethers, parachutes, or other attachments;
- anything else on board or attached at the moment of takeoff.
If the aircraft is 54.9 lb before you attach a 0.2 lb item, it is over the limit. If it is 55.0 lb at takeoff but lands lighter, it still fails because the rule measures at takeoff.

4. BOUNDARY TABLE
Weight on takeoff (all on board or attached) | Small UAS?
< 55 lb | Yes
55.0 lb | No
> 55 lb | No

Examples:
- 54.999 lb: qualifies.
- 55.000 lb: does not qualify.
- 25.000 kg (55.1156 lb): does not qualify.

5. SECONDARY THRESHOLD: 0.55 LB / 250 G
0.55 lb is the Part 107 Category 1 operations-over-people threshold, not the general small-UAS definition. Category 1 requires the aircraft to weigh 0.55 lb or less on takeoff and throughout the duration of each operation, including everything on board or attached. Category 1 also has a non-weight condition: no exposed rotating parts that would lacerate human skin. 0.55 lb = 249.48 g; 250 g = 0.55116 lb, which is slightly over 0.55 lb. For a strict Category 1 margin, use 249 g or less. Category 2 and Category 3 operations over people use kinetic-energy limits, not a simple weight limit; do not use 55 lb for those.

6. WHAT CHANGES ABOVE 55 LB
Above 55 lb, the aircraft is not a 'small unmanned aircraft,' so Part 107 does not apply. You need other FAA authority, such as:
- an exemption under 49 U.S.C. § 44807 (special authority for certain UAS); or
- an airworthiness certificate and operation under Part 91 (for example, experimental category); or
- public aircraft operation if eligible.
A Part 107 waiver cannot fix this: the 55 lb limit is in the definition of 'small unmanned aircraft,' not an operational rule that can be waived under 14 CFR § 107.205. Operating a UAS of 55 lb or more without the appropriate authority is not authorized.

7. RECREATIONAL VS PART 107
The request says 'FAA rules.' The Part 107 definition in 14 CFR § 107.3 is the operative FAA definition of 'small unmanned aircraft' and is the source of the 55 lb figure. Recreational operations under 49 U.S.C. § 44809 are a separate statutory exception with their own conditions; confirm those conditions before flying. That exception does not create a larger small-UAS weight class.

8. REGISTRATION AND REMOTE ID NOTES
FAA guidance generally requires registration for UAS weighing more than 0.55 lb; at or below 0.55 lb, registration is generally not required. Confirm the current Part 48 and Part 107 registration rules for your operation. Remote ID requirements generally attach to UAS that require registration; confirm applicability for the specific aircraft and operation.

9. COMPLIANCE CHECKLIST
[ ] Weigh the aircraft in its heaviest takeoff configuration, including all attachments and payload.
[ ] Use a calibrated scale and record the result.
[ ] Compare to 55.000 lb; the aircraft must be strictly below 55.000 lb.
[ ] If using kg, compare to 24.9476 kg; use 24.9 kg or less. Do not use 25 kg.
[ ] If using Category 1, compare to 0.55 lb (249.48 g); use 249 g or less for margin.
[ ] Register the UAS if required; generally this applies above 0.55 lb.
[ ] Confirm Remote ID compliance if applicable.
[ ] If the aircraft is 55 lb or more, stop and obtain the appropriate FAA authority before operation.
[ ] Check state and local rules for any lower limits.

10. SOURCES
- 14 CFR § 107.3 (definition of small unmanned aircraft).
- 14 CFR Part 107 Subpart D (Category 1, 0.55 lb).
- FAA Part 107 guidance and FAA AIM Chapter 11, Section 1.
- 49 U.S.C. § 44807 (above-threshold authority).
- 49 U.S.C. § 44809 (recreational exception).

This answer covers U.S. federal FAA rules only. State and local rules may be more restrictive.

answer:
BASIC VFR WEATHER MINIMUMS — CLASS E AIRSPACE BELOW 10,000 FT MSL (U.S. FAA, 14 CFR 91.155)

ANSWER
  Flight visibility:      3 statute miles
  Distance from clouds:   500 feet below
                          1,000 feet above
                          2,000 feet horizontal

GOVERNING RULE
14 CFR § 91.155(a), "Basic VFR weather minimums." The table entry reads: Class E, Less than 10,000 feet MSL — Flight visibility 3 statute miles; Distance from clouds: 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, 2,000 feet horizontal. The same minimums are reproduced in the FAA Aeronautical Information Manual (AIM), Chapter 3, Section 1 (Airspace), and are the figures an examiner or briefer will quote.

UNITS
Visibility is expressed in statute miles (not nautical miles, not km); cloud clearance in feet. These are the units the regulation itself uses.

APPLICATION NOTES (read before using the numbers)
1. Airspeed is irrelevant below 10,000 ft MSL. The 250-knot split ("at or below 250 knots" vs "above 250 knots") appears in the table only for Class E and Class G airspace AT OR ABOVE 10,000 ft MSL. Below 10,000 ft MSL there is one uniform set of numbers, as stated above.
2. No day/night difference in Class E. Unlike Class G — where the minimums change at night and with altitude — Class E below 10,000 ft MSL carries the same 3 SM / 500-1,000-2,000 requirement day and night. (Night currency and equipment rules under 91.205 and 91.109 are separate matters and do not change 91.155's Class E numbers.)
3. Class E surface areas: there is no separate, stricter basic-VFR minimum in 91.155 for Class E that extends to the surface. The same 3 SM / 500 below / 1,000 above / 2,000 horizontal applies. What changes in a surface area is the need for an ATC clearance/communication only if the surface area is also associated with a Class D or Class C airport; the weather minimum itself is unchanged. (Do not confuse this with Class B, which is 3 SM and clear of clouds, or Class C and D, which are 3 SM / 500 below / 1,000 above / 2,000 horizontal.)
4. For contrast only — Class E AT OR ABOVE 10,000 ft MSL: 5 statute miles visibility, 1,000 feet below, 1,000 feet above, 1 statute mile horizontal (and above 250 knots: 5 SM, 1,000 below, 1,000 above, 1 SM horizontal). These figures do NOT apply to the below-10,000-ft case asked about; they are listed solely so the 3 SM figure is not mistakenly applied above 10,000 ft or vice versa.
5. Class G is not Class E. If the flight is in Class G airspace, different minimums apply (1 SM day / 3 SM night at or below 1,200 ft AGL, etc.). Confirm the airspace classification on the sectional before applying the figures above.

EXCEPTIONS AND CAVEATS (per 91.155(b) and 91.157)
The 3 SM / 500-1,000-2,000 minimum is the baseline. It is subject to the exceptions in § 91.155(b) (e.g., operations in Class G at or below 1,200 ft AGL day/night, helicopters, airports with prescribed traffic patterns) and to Special VFR under § 91.157, which permits ground visibility as low as 1 statute mile and clear of clouds in surface areas with an ATC clearance. Special VFR, SVFR at night (instrument rating and instrument-equipped aircraft required), and any applicable waivers are outside the "basic" minimum and are not part of the answer above.

SOURCES
- 14 CFR § 91.155 (eCFR, current): http://ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-91.155
- FAA AIM, Chapter 3, Section 1 — Airspace: https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/aim_html/chap3_section_1.html

JURISDICTION
Figures are U.S. FAA (FAR Part 91). Other authorities (EASA, ICAO Annex 2, etc.) use different values and metric units; those numbers are not interchangeable with the ones above.

answer:
SAFETY ENGINEER'S ANSWER — OSHA PEL AND ACTION LEVEL FOR RESPIRABLE CRYSTALLINE SILICA, GENERAL INDUSTRY

1. DIRECT ANSWER

| Quantity | Value (8-hr TWA) | Equivalent | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Permissible Exposure Limit (PEL) | 50 µg/m³ | 0.050 mg/m³ | 29 CFR 1910.1053(c)(1) |
| Action Level (AL) | 25 µg/m³ | 0.025 mg/m³ | 29 CFR 1910.1053(b) (definition of "action level") |

Both are airborne concentrations of respirable crystalline silica, calculated as 8-hour time-weighted averages (TWA). The AL is exactly one-half the PEL. The governing standard for general industry is 29 CFR 1910.1053, "Respirable crystalline silica" (the same section OSHA applies to maritime employment other than shipyard employment, which has a parallel section at 29 CFR 1915.1053 with identical numeric limits).

2. REGULATORY BASIS (operative language, in substance)

1910.1053(c)(1) — Permissible exposure limit: "The employer shall ensure that no employee is exposed to an airborne concentration of respirable crystalline silica in excess of 50 µg/m³, calculated as an 8-hour TWA."

1910.1053(b) — Action level: "...an airborne concentration of respirable crystalline silica of 25 µg/m³, calculated as an 8-hour TWA."

1910.1053(b) — 8-hour TWA: employee exposure over an 8-hour work shift, computed as the sum of (concentration × duration) for each sampled interval divided by 8 hours, i.e. TWA = Σ(Ci·Ti)/8. A shift longer than 8 hours is still evaluated on an 8-hour TWA basis, but the additional exposure hours must be captured in the summation — a 12-hour shift at a steady 40 µg/m³ yields a TWA of 60 µg/m³ and is an overexposure, not a compliant 40 µg/m³.

VERIFICATION NOTE (carry this into use): the two research retrievals behind this memo returned the same values but neither captured a quoted passage from the eCFR/OSHA page. The values above are stated from established knowledge of the standard and are consistent with those retrievals, but before this figure is used in an enforcement-facing document, confirm it by opening https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/section-1910.1053 and reading paragraphs (b) and (c)(1). This is a 2-minute check and it is the only open item in this memo.

3. SCOPE — WHY 1910.1053 AND NOT THE OTHER SILICA SECTIONS

OSHA's 2016 respirable crystalline silica rulemaking produced three parallel standards, all with the same numeric limits but different compliance mechanics:
- 29 CFR 1910.1053 — general industry and maritime (the answer to this request)
- 29 CFR 1915.1053 — shipyard employment
- 29 CFR 1926.1153 — construction (compliance typically via Table 1 specified engineering controls/methods rather than a standalone exposure assessment)
If your operation is general industry, 1910.1053 governs and the PEL is 50 µg/m³. Do not cite 1926.1153 for a general-industry facility even though its numbers are identical; the citation is what gets challenged in an inspection or a grievance.

State-plan states: OSHA-approved State Plans must be at least as effective as the federal standard but may be stricter. Confirm the state limit before finalizing; a handful of states have adopted or considered more protective occupational limits for silica. Federal OSHA values apply directly in federal-program states and in federal jurisdiction.

4. WHAT THE TWO NUMBERS TRIGGER (practical compliance consequence)

- Exposure assessment (1910.1053(d)): the employer must assess each employee's exposure using either the performance option (objective data or air monitoring representative of the employee's exposure) or the scheduled monitoring option. Assessment is required for employees who may reasonably be expected to be exposed at or above the AL.
- Monitoring frequency (scheduled monitoring option): if the measured exposure is at or above the AL but at or below the PEL, repeat monitoring within 6 months; if above the PEL, repeat within 3 months. Repeat monitoring may be discontinued under the conditions in (d)(3).
- Notification: employees must be notified in writing within 30 days of any monitoring result that is at or above the AL, and of the corrective action being taken, when results exceed the PEL.
- Engineering and work-practice controls (1910.1053(f)): required where exposures exceed the PEL; respirators only as an interim or supplementary measure, and required where controls are not feasible or do not fully reduce exposure to the PEL.
- Respiratory protection program (1910.1053(g)): required whenever respirators are used; the assigned protection factor must reduce the TWA to at or below 50 µg/m³. Example: a measured 180 µg/m³ TWA requires a respirator with an APF of at least 4 (half-mask, minimum) — and controls, not just the respirator, because the PEL is exceeded.
- Medical surveillance (1910.1053(i)): offered to employees who will be exposed at or above the AL for 30 or more days per year; includes baseline and periodic exams, TB testing where indicated, and the silica-specific medical questionnaire.
- Housekeeping (1910.1053(h)): no dry sweeping or dry brushing where such activity could contribute to exposure; no compressed air for cleaning unless combined with ventilation that captures the dust.
- Training (1910.1053(j)): required for employees exposed at or above the AL.
- Written exposure control plan (1910.1053(f)(2) / (g)): required where exposures exceed the PEL — describe tasks, engineering controls, work practices, and housekeeping.

5. COMMON ERRORS TO AVOID WHEN APPLYING THESE NUMBERS

- Unit confusion: the silica PEL is 50 µg/m³, not 50 mg/m³ and not 0.05 mg/m³. 0.05 mg/m³ is the correct equivalent only when written as mg/m³. Lab reports frequently come back in mg/m³; convert before comparing to the PEL (multiply mg/m³ by 1000 to get µg/m³).
- Using the pre-2016 formula PEL: the old Table Z-3 limit for respirable quartz was 10 mg/m³ ÷ (%SiO2 + 2) — roughly 98 µg/m³ at 100% quartz. That formula was removed for crystalline silica by the 2016 rule and must not be used for compliance. It is looser than 50 µg/m³ and citing it would understate the requirement.
- Treating the AL as a limit: 25 µg/m³ is not the compliance ceiling; it is the trigger for assessment, monitoring, medical surveillance, and training. Exposures between 25 and 50 µg/m³ are compliant but regulated.
- Sampling convention: "respirable" means the ISO/CEN respirable aerosol convention. Use a cyclone meeting that convention (e.g., 4 µm aluminum cyclone at 2.5 L/min, or GK2.69 at 4.2 L/min) and analysis by XRD (NIOSH 7500) or IR (NIOSH 7602/7603). Total dust or a non-respirable sample cannot be compared to 50 µg/m³.
- Polymorphs: the standard covers respirable crystalline silica generally (quartz, cristobalite, tridymite); there is no separate numeric limit per polymorph, so do not split the sample and apply different thresholds.

6. VERIFICATION STEPS BEFORE PUBLICATION

1. Open eCFR 29 CFR 1910.1053 and read (b) and (c)(1) to confirm 50 µg/m³ and 25 µg/m³, both 8-hr TWA. (Closes the one open item in this memo.)
2. Confirm jurisdiction: federal OSHA or a State Plan, and if a State Plan, confirm whether it has adopted a different value.
3. Confirm the sector: 1910.1053 (general industry/maritime), 1915.1053 (shipyards), or 1926.1153 (construction).
4. Confirm the intended use — compliance planning, exposure assessment, or general reference — and pull in the ancillary obligations in Section 4 that the use case requires.

## Answer

NVD assigns **CVE-2021-44228** a **CVSS v3.1 base score of 10.0** with severity **CRITICAL**.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| CVE | CVE-2021-44228 (Apache Log4j 2 / Log4Shell) |
| CVSS version | 3.1 |
| Base score | **10.0** |
| Severity | **CRITICAL** |
| Vector string | `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H` |
| Metric source | NVD (Primary/NVD-assigned v3.1 metric) |

Severity is derived from the score per the CVSS v3.1 qualitative rating scale (None 0.0, Low 0.1-3.9, Medium 4.0-6.9, High 7.0-8.9, Critical 9.0-10.0); 10.0 sits on the inclusive upper bound of the Critical band.

## Independent recomputation from the vector (spec check, not a quote)

This is the verification that the published number is self-consistent with the vector string. CVSS v3.1 weights used:

- AV:N = 0.85; AC:L = 0.77; PR:N (Scope Changed) = 0.85; UI:N = 0.85
- C:H = I:H = A:H = 0.56
- Scope = Changed (S:C) -> use the changed-scope branch and the 1.08 multiplier

Step 1 - Impact Sub-Score (ISS):
```
ISS = 1 - [(1-C)(1-I)(1-A)]
    = 1 - (0.44 * 0.44 * 0.44)
    = 1 - 0.085184
    = 0.914816
```

Step 2 - Impact (Scope Changed branch):
```
Impact = 7.52 * (ISS - 0.029) - 3.25 * (ISS - 0.02)^15
       = 7.52 * 0.885816 - 3.25 * (0.894816)^15
       = 6.66134 - 3.25 * 0.18883
       = 6.66134 - 0.61370
       = 6.04764
```

Step 3 - Exploitability:
```
Exploitability = 8.22 * AV * AC * PR * UI
               = 8.22 * 0.85 * 0.77 * 0.85 * 0.85
               = 8.22 * 0.472876
               = 3.88704
```

Step 4 - Base score (Scope Changed):
```
raw  = 1.08 * (Impact + Exploitability)
     = 1.08 * (6.04764 + 3.88704)
     = 1.08 * 9.93468
     = 10.7295
Base = Roundup(min(raw, 10))
     = Roundup(min(10.7295, 10))
     = Roundup(10)
     = 10.0
```

Note for anyone re-deriving this by hand: the uncapped intermediate is **10.73**, which exceeds the CVSS v3.1 maximum of 10.0. The `min(...,10)` clamp in the spec is what produces the correct 10.0; citing 10.7 or 10.8 would be an error. The result is 10.0 exactly, so `Roundup` does not push it past the scale maximum.

## Reproducible retrieval (so the figure can be re-attributed to a date)

NVD metrics change over time, and this CVE in particular was re-scored during its life (an earlier NVD v3.1 assessment used `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H`, which computes to 9.8; the current assessment uses `S:C`, which computes to 10.0). The 10.0/CRITICAL figure above is therefore stated as the NVD-assigned v3.1 metric, and should be cited with the retrieval date.

Query via the NVD CVE API 2.0 (no key required, but rate-limited to 5 requests / 30 s without one):

```bash
curl -s -H 'Accept: application/json' \
  'https://services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0?cveId=CVE-2021-44228' \
| jq -r '.vulnerabilities[0].cve |
    "status=" + (.vulnStatus // "n/a") +
    " published=" + (.published // "n/a") +
    " lastModified=" + (.lastModified // "n/a"),
    (.metrics.cvssMetricV31[]?
      | "type=" + .type +
        " source=" + .cvssData.baseScore.ToString + " " + (.source // "n/a") +
        " score=" + (.cvssData.baseScore|tostring) +
        " severity=" + (.cvssData.baseSeverity // "n/a") +
        " vector=" + .cvssData.vectorString)'
```

1. Use the entry with `type = "Primary"` - that is the NVD-assigned metric. `type = "Secondary"` entries are CNA/supplier-provided and **must not** be conflated with NVD's score.
2. Confirm `cvssData.version = "3.1"`; the record may also carry a `cvssMetricV2` block, which is out of scope here.
3. Confirm `vulnStatus` is not `Rejected`, and check `cveDescription`/the NVD detail page for any `** DISPUTED **` annotation. If a dispute or re-score has appeared, the score above is superseded and must be re-derived by the procedure in this document (recompute from the new `vectorString`).
4. Record `published`, `lastModified`, and the retrieval timestamp alongside the score.

## Scope and caveats

- **Score answered: 10.0. Severity: CRITICAL.** These are the NVD-assigned CVSS v3.1 figures, not a CNA/supplier score, and not the CVSS v2.0 score that also appears in the NVD record.
- The one thing not independently verifiable from the material available here is whether NVD has since annotated the entry as disputed or re-scored it again. This does not block the numeric answer (all NVD data in hand gives 10.0 with the `S:C` vector), but it is the reason the retrieval procedure and date attribution above are part of the deliverable rather than optional extras. Re-run step 1-4 before publishing the figure in any downstream artifact.

ANSWER

Under the 1876 first edition of Robert's Rules of Order (the pocket manual carried by Project Gutenberg as eBook #9097), a motion for the Previous Question requires a TWO-THIRDS VOTE for adoption. It is not a majority vote.

VERBATIM SOURCE TEXT

The manual's own words on the motion:

  "It shall require a two-thirds vote for its adoption."

That sentence appears in the manual's treatment of the Previous Question (the motion to cut off debate and take the vote immediately). The same two-thirds requirement is reflected in the manual's tabular summary of the rules relating to motions, where the Previous Question is listed with a two-thirds vote requirement — so the manual states the rule twice: once in the body text of the Previous Question section and once in the summary table. Both agree; there is no internal inconsistency in the manual to reconcile.

HOW TO VERIFY (reproducible procedure)

1. Open Project Gutenberg eBook #9097, Robert's Rules of Order (Henry M. Robert), preferably the plain-text or HTML file: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/9097 (text at https://www.gutenberg.org/files/9097/9097-0.txt or https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/9097/pg9097-images.html).
2. Search the text for "Previous Question" — the motion has its own numbered section in Part I (Rules of Order).
3. Within that section, locate the sentence "It shall require a two-thirds vote for its adoption." Confirm it sits inside the Previous Question section, not in a neighbouring motion's section.
4. Cross-check against the manual's table/summary of rules relating to motions (near the end of the Rules of Order), where the Previous Question's vote column reads two-thirds.
5. Record the section heading and running head from the Gutenberg file as the citation anchor.

CITATION

The authority is the section of the 1876 manual devoted to the Previous Question (in the 1876 numbering, Art. IV, § 20 — the section number should be confirmed against the running heads of the Gutenberg file rather than taken from memory, since the quotation above is the load-bearing evidence and the numbering is only a locator).

SCOPE, AND WHAT THIS ANSWER DOES NOT ESTABLISH

- It answers for the 1876 text as carried by Project Gutenberg, i.e., the rule as originally written, not as later amended in subsequent editions of Robert's Rules.
- It states the fraction required (two-thirds). It does not, on the verified quotation alone, establish the base against which the two-thirds is counted (members present versus votes cast). That definition lives in the manual's general definitions/early articles and was not captured verbatim in the material checked; a reader who needs the base should read that definitions passage directly in the Gutenberg text before relying on any particular base.
- The edition-status question (whether the Gutenberg transcription reproduces the true 1876 first printing or a later corrected printing) was flagged as unverified in the research. It does not change the answer: the two-thirds requirement for the Previous Question is stable across the 1876 text and later authoritative editions, so the answer holds under either reading of the edition question.
- The motion's accompanying characteristics (that it must be seconded, is not debatable, and is not amendable) are consistent with the manual's treatment but are not the question asked and are not offered here as quoted findings.
- No discrepancy with modern practice needs reconciling on this point: the current official Robert's Rules standard also requires a two-thirds vote for the Previous Question. The manual and modern practice agree, so the answer is the same whether read historically or currently — but the authority for this answer is the 1876 manual itself.

BOTTOM LINE FOR THE RECORD

Required vote to adopt the Previous Question under the 1876 manual: two-thirds.

question: H13
answer:
SOURCE AND SCOPE
Authority: BIPM, Le Système international d'unités / The International System of Units (SI), 9th edition, 2019 — the English text published by the BIPM. The governing passage is the definition of the photometric base unit, the candela, in the chapter on SI units (Table 4 / the defining-constants section), not a derived or contextual mention elsewhere in the Brochure.

DEFINING TEXT (as it bears on the two asks)
"... This definition implies the exact relation Kcd = 683 cd sr kg−1 m−2 s3 for monochromatic radiation of frequency ν = 540 × 1012 Hz."

ANSWER 1 — FIXED VALUE OF THE LUMINOUS EFFICACY
Kcd = 683
Unit: lm W−1 (lumens per watt).
Exact equivalent forms given by the same definition and usable interchangeably:
  683 lm W−1
  683 cd sr W−1
  683 cd sr kg−1 m−2 s3
Status: exact by definition. It is a defining constant of the revised SI; it carries no uncertainty and no measurement error bar, and it is not a measured quantity. It should be written 683, not 683.0 or 683.00, since trailing zeros would imply a resolution the definition does not have.

ANSWER 2 — FREQUENCY OF THE MONOCHROMATIC RADIATION
ν = 540 × 10^12 Hz
Unit: Hz (hertz, s−1).
Equivalent restatement: 540 THz.
Status: exact by definition, fixed in the same sentence as the 683 value; the pair (683 lm W−1 at 540 × 10^12 Hz) is the complete definitional content.

HOW THE TWO NUMBERS RELATE (so they are not misread as independent)
The efficacy value and the frequency are a single definitional pair: 683 lm W−1 is the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation *at* 540 × 10^12 Hz. Neither number is meaningful as a specification without the other. The candela is defined as the luminous intensity, in a given direction, of a source that emits monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10^12 Hz and that has a radiant intensity in that direction of (1/683) W sr−1 — the (1/683) W sr−1 is the same 683 stated from the radiometric side.

NOTE ON FREQUENCY VERSUS WAVELENGTH (guard against a common error)
The Brochure fixes the defining quantity by *frequency*, 540 × 10^12 Hz. The often-quoted figure of approximately 555 nm is a derived correspondence to that frequency in standard air, not a fixed defining value, and it is not what the Brochure states. Any downstream document that substitutes "555 nm" for "540 × 10^12 Hz" as the defining condition is departing from the source text; if a wavelength is quoted at all it must be labelled as an approximate, medium-dependent equivalent.

PRESENTATION RULES FOR THE DELIVERABLE TEXT
1. Quote 683 with unit lm W−1 (optionally also cd sr kg−1 m−2 s3) and state explicitly that it is exact.
2. Quote 540 × 10^12 Hz (optionally also 540 THz) and state explicitly that it is exact and that it is a frequency.
3. Do not attach an uncertainty, a ± term, or a significant-figure caveat to either number.
4. Attribute both to the SI Brochure, 9th edition (2019), BIPM, candela definition.
5. If a later amendment or errata to the 9th edition is invoked, re-verify the wording; as of the researched source fetch, the 683 lm W−1 at 540 × 10^12 Hz statement is the authoritative text and no disagreement was found among the BIPM sources consulted (full Brochure, concise Brochure, and the BIPM SI Appendix 2 sheet on the candela).

CONDENSED ANSWER AS IT WOULD APPE AR IN THE DOCUMENT
The SI Brochure, 9th edition (BIPM, 2019), fixes the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation, Kcd, at exactly 683 lm W−1 (equivalently 683 cd sr kg−1 m−2 s3) for monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10^12 Hz (540 THz). Both values are exact by definition.
